5. Experiments                                                   5.3. Qualitative Results and Analysis
5.1. Tasks, Settings and Metrics
Tasks. To demonstrate the superiority of our framework,
we select 2 representative tasks from DeformableRavens
benchmark: (1) cable-ring: manipulating a ring to a given
green circle, (2) cable-ring-notarget: manipulating a ring
to any circle, as well as 2 representative tasks from SoftGym:
(3) SpreadCloth: spreading crumpled cloth to be flat, (4)
RopeConfiguration: manipulating a rope from a random
pose to a target pose (we use the shape ‘S’ as the target).
Among them, the first two are relatively easier. They can be
accomplished without considering future actions and states,
and we conduct them to show our dense affordance’s supe-
riority over methods imitating expert demonstrations. The
last two are much harder and would be better accomplished
considering future actions and states to avoid local optima.
Settings. For all tasks, in both training and testing, we set    Figure 6. Example action sequences for cable-ring, cable-ring-
different random seeds for each episode, producing unseen        notarget, SpreadCloth and RopeConfiguration. White point de-

ization ability between our proposed dense affordance and
                                                                    Figure 6 shows examples of manipulation trajectories for
imitation-based methods, for cables in DeformableRavens,
                                                                 diverse tasks using our proposed affordance. It is worth
we directly test the model trained on cables with 32 beads
                                                                 mentioning that, in the second state of SpreadCloth (Row
over novel cable configurations with 24, 28 or 36 beads.
                                                                 3), though it is intuitive to place the picking point (white)
Metrics. For cable-ring and cable-ring-notarget, we fol-
                                                                 to the top-left position, the model places it to the bottom-
low DeformableRavens and use the manipulation successful

rate as the metric. For SpreadCloth and RopeConfiguration,
                                                                 low coverage but high ‘value’, requiring only one follow-
we follow SoftGym and use the normalized score as the met-
                                                                 ing pick-and-place action to almost fully unfold the cloth.
ric. For all tasks, higher scores indicate better performance.
5.2. Baselines
   For two cable-ring related tasks, we compare our method
with baselines with or without expert demonstrations:
   • Transporter [47, 38] is commonly used for robotic
     manipulation by learning visual correlation for pick-
     ing and placing points. In DeformableRavens [38] it is
     trained by cloning expert demonstrations and achieves
     SOTA performance over relevant tasks.
   • GT-State receives ground truth (GT) pose of the target
     object, and regresses ppick and pplace with MLP.
   • GT-State 2-Step first regresses ppick and then pplace
     using ppick and GT pose concatenation, both via MLP.
   For SpreadCloth and RopeConfiguration, as object states       Picking                Placing Picking                  Placing
and dynamics are too complex and the tasks are too difficult     Figure 7. Picking and placing affordance. Each row contains two
to hand-engineer expert policies, we compare our method          (picking affordance, observation with ppick , placing affordance)
with baselines focused on multi-step planning:                   tuples for a task. ppick is selected by picking affordance. Higher
   • CURL-SAC [23] that uses a model-free RL approach            color temperature means higher affordance.
     with contrastive unsupervised representations.
   • DrQ[46] applies augmentation, regularization to RL.             Figure 7 visualizes picking and placing affordance,
                                                                 clearly showing that the learned affordance represents de-
   • PlaNet [16] learns state space dynamics for planning.
                                                                 formable objects with complex states and dynamics and fa-
   • MVP [45] learns pick-and-place policy with model-
                                                                 cilitates selecting picking and placing points for manipula-
     free RL designed for deformbale object manipulation.
                                                                 tion. Figure 8 visualizes ‘value’s of states.

                                                                   6. Conclusion
Figure 10. Picking and placing affordance before (middle) and
after (right) IST of the observation (left). White: pick point.
                                                                       We propose to use dense visual affordance for manipu-
                                                                   lating deformable objects with complex states and dynam-
                                                                   ics. For tasks that require a series of strongly related ac-
5.6. Real-world Experiments
                                                                   tions, we further empower the proposed affordance with the
   To bridge the sim2real gap and implement our method in          awareness of a certain action’s influence on subsequent ac-
the real world, similar to [45, 15], we use domain random-         tions. We propose a self-supervised framework with novel
ization to train affordance models in simulation and fine-         designs to efficiently collect multi-stage interaction data and
tune them in real world. Specifically, we collect real-world       stably learn this representation. Experiments on representa-
data using Fold to Unfold, fine-tune trained-in-simulation         tive tasks and in the real world show the superiority of our
Mpick and Mplace stage by stage using the collected data.          proposed dense affordance and the learning framework.

                                                                    Therefore, the trained dense affordance could represent the
                                                                    distribution of diverse results of diverse actions. Each inter-
                                                                    action data contains the actions (picking point and placing

D.2. Real-world Data Collection and Fine-tuning
    As the configurations, kinematics and dynamics of de-
formable objects (like cloth and ropes) in the real world are
different from those in simulation, we fine-tune the trained-
in-simulation affordance using real-world collected interac-
tions.
    Specifically, following Section 4.5 (Fold to Unfold: Ef-
ficient Multi-stage Data Collection for Learning Fore-
sightful Affordance) in the main paper, we collect real-
world interactions using the Fold-to-Unfold method in dif-
ferent stages (demonstrations shown in Figure 14). For fine-
tuning, we tune the learned picking and placing affordance
stage-by-stage using the above real-world collected data.




Figure 14. Demonstrations of real-world collected data. State
oi+1 shows the starting state and state o′i show the ending state of
interaction data for training.
